Life Magazine. Launched in 1936 by Henry Luce, Life pioneered the picture-magazine format and became the dominant visual chronicle of American life and world events. The first issue featured striking color photography of everyday American life. Life pioneered the photo-essay format, using sequences of carefully curated images to tell stories with minimal text. Peak circulation reached nearly thirteen million in the mid-1970s, making it the most widely read magazine ever published. The magazine documented major historical events through photography. It chronicled World War II, the space program, the Vietnam War, and the civil rights movement. Life employed famous photographers including Margaret Bourke-White, Alfred Eisenstaedt, and John Dominis. The magazine became famous for its bold, luxurious color photography and dramatic layouts that set the standard for visual magazines. It published continuously for thirty-six years before suspending in 1972, then revived in 1978 as a monthly publication. Through its visual innovation, Life exemplified and elevated the art of photojournalism and defined how Americans visualized their era.
